Concretely, four things.

A monthly load factor tracker by route against a ramp curve — say 55% in month three, 62% by month six, 70% by month twelve — reviewed by the CEO, not buried in ops reporting. Booking curve data is the leading indicator: you see 60-90 days out whether a month will miss, so you're not learning after the fact.

Second, a written trigger. If forward bookings on either new route are more than five points below the curve at the six-month checkpoint, you cut frequency on that route and don't add the planned flights. Decide the rule now, before anyone's emotionally invested.

Third, keep the aircraft flexible. Don't commit all 5,000 flights in the schedule up front — hold back maybe a third of the capacity so it can go to the four healthy routes, or charter, if the new cities disappoint.

Fourth, stage the exits so Lakeport and Port Avery still run reduced frequency through the ramp, giving you a fallback and preserving some connecting feed.
